newsitem.title: PERU: No quick end seen as Lima crisis hits third month.
newsitem.headline: No quick end seen as Lima crisis hits third month.

text.p: The Lima hostage crisis reached its three-month milestone on Monday with prospects still distant for an end to the grueling ordeal for 72 dignitaries held under the gun by Peru's Marxist rebels.
In a short speech on the 90th day of the siege, President Alberto Fujimori had little to offer his country beyond lamenting the captives' plight as a "terrible situation."
Families of the hostages holed up in the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence staged a day of solidarity, including a noisy nationwide demonstration at midday.
In a chaotic cacophany outside the residence, car owners set off their alarms, neighbours came out to bang pots, pans and bottles, and demonstrators blew whistles and chanted.
In the surrounding San Isidro neighbourhood -- as throughout Peru -- churches held special masses and rang bells in a sign of support for the captives.
Motorists in Lima sounded horns, and legislators came out of Congress to hold a minute's silence in a nearby square before applauding and shouting for the hostages' freedom.
"I hope that inside they all feel that we are with them, that we love them," said Beatriz de Gumucio, wife of captive Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio, outside the residence.

"I am moved by the displays of solidarity. The whole of Peru has united for this group of 72 dignified people," said Luisa Aguilar, wife of captive judge Hugo Sivina. "I am sure that the terrorists have heard us and realised that there is no room for them in this country. Nobody is with them."
Some of the hostages responded by raising hands to a window sandwiched between a rebel flag and a banner railing against Fujimori. One of them waved a white handkerchief.
An open letter from the families described the time since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) takeover of the diplomatic compound as "three months of agony and suffering."

More than 500 hostages were taken on Dec. 17 when some 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall, swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout and took control. But the MRTA gradually released most of its prisoners, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips in its central aim of freeing some 400 jailed comrades.

The remaining captives -- top diplomats, security chiefs, ministers, judges and businessmen -- are mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, intelligence and medical reports say. Stress, gum diseases and skin ailments are common.

The hostages have already passed Christmas and New Year inside the cramped building with the windows closed and no air conditioning despite the hot Lima summer. They look likely to spend Easter there, too.

"The basic problem is now almost the same as 90 days ago -- how to deal with the demand for freedom of MRTA prisoners. No political way to deal with this has yet been found," former captive and opposition legislator Javier Diez Canseco, released in the early days of the crisis, told Reuters.
"I think of the hostages every day, of what they are going through," he added.

Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar sent a greeting to Gumucio and called for the three-month milestone to be used as a time for reflection. "Ninety days is too much. However, there is no short-term solution in sight," he said in a phone conversation from La Paz with a local radio station.

Members of a three-man guarantors commission overseeing negotiations between the government and rebels were expected to meet later Monday with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas, local radio said.

The guarantors are meeting separately with the MRTA and government negotiator Domingo Palermo in an effort to pave the way for a negotiated solution after 10 rounds of face-to-face talks apparently brought little more than a polite exchange of divergent positions.

Pollster Apoyo S.A. released a survey showing that more than half of Peruvians believed the crisis -- already Latin America's longest hostage siege -- would take at least one month more to resolve. Thirty-three percent of those surveyed believed the crisis would last another one to three months, while 20 percent thought it would take more than three months.
